extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, mathematics teachers, and graduate students in math education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and analytic frameworks for researching, teaching, and evaluating students' and teachers' understandings of mathematical proof (what counts as proof, what convinces, and classroom practices that support proof). Emphasizes theoretical constructs, common misconceptions, and methodological recommendations for studying conviction and proof-related activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive arguments as the mathematician's standard of conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the 'proving as convincing' perspective, instruction aims for students to be convinced by the same types of evidence as mathematicians — specifically deductive arguments (i.e., arguments using valid modes of argumentation as specified in the chapter's definition of proof) rather than empirical evidence or appeals to authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional goal: help students recognize limitations of empirical or authoritative evidence and to attain high (or absolute) conviction via deductive arguments. Research often investigates whether students' standards align with those of the mathematical community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical argument (invalid as proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical argument purports to show the truth of a statement by verifying a proper subset of the cases covered by the statement (e.g., checking several examples) and thus fails to meet the standard of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical arguments as invalid modes of proof in formal instruction/research. Balacheff's 'naïve empiricism' and 'crucial experiment' and Harel & Sowder's 'empirical justification scheme' are examples. Research should account for students' propensity to produce and accept these arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balacheff's hierarchy of argument types
rubrics_metrics.description: Four main argument types privileged in cognitive development of proof: (1) naïve empiricism — accept based on a few confirming cases; (2) crucial experiment — accept based on verification in carefully selected test cases; (3) generic example — establish truth via operations on a representative particular case; (4) thought experiment — establish truth via internalized action detached from particular representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify student arguments and to track developmental progress. Note that 'crucial experiment' is more sophisticated than 'naïve empiricism', and 'generic example' can serve as a bridge toward deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harel & Sowder's justification (proof) schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of what convinces students (and what they offer) into three major categories with subcategories: (1) externally-based — conviction from authority, form, or meaningless symbol manipulation (authoritarian, ritual, non-referential symbolic); (2) empirical — conviction from examples or perceptual evidence (examples-based/inductive, perceptual); (3) deductive/analytic — conviction from general reasoning or logical deduction (transformational, axiomatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these schemes to analyze student justifications; use subcategories to pinpoint sources of conviction (e.g., ritual/formal reasoning vs true deductive insight). Helpful when designing interventions to shift students toward deductive schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic argument / generic proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic argument establishes a claim by reasoning about a generic (representative, non-special) element of a set so that the reasoning generalizes to any element; frequently used as an intermediate between empirical arguments and formal deductive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize generic arguments as pedagogically useful — they are concrete and accessible for students and can bridge to fully general deductive proofs. Distinguish them from mere examples and emphasize how generalizability is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain/applicability constraint of current frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing analytic frameworks (Balacheff; Harel & Sowder; Marrades & Gutiérrez) are more applicable to tasks that justify true statements over infinite sets (e.g., algebraic generalizations) and less apt for tasks involving refutation of false statements, finite-set claims, or techniques like disproof by counterexample and proof by exhaustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and instructors should adapt or expand frameworks to capture arguments used in refutation, finite cases, and other proof techniques not well-represented in existing taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the power of counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Students (and some teachers) should recognize that a single counterexample conclusively refutes a generalization; failing to accept this shows a misunderstanding of proof by counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should target students' tendencies to dismiss counterexamples as special cases; assessment should probe whether learners accept the refutational power of one counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding implications, converses, inverses, and contrapositives
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners should correctly understand logical relations: a conditional statement is not generally equivalent to its converse or inverse, while it is equivalent to its contrapositive; many students and teachers are mistakenly convinced otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comprehension of these logical principles explicitly (symbolic and verbal forms), since misunderstandings persist across levels and contexts; design tasks that reveal confusion between implication and its related forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep (not superficial) understanding of mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should grasp the logical underpinnings and scope of proof by mathematical induction rather than relying on superficial cues (e.g., familiarity with the method or its use in similar examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of acceptance of inductive proofs based on method recognition alone; probe whether learners appreciate boundary-of-domain issues and the generalization mechanism in induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving as socially embedded — proofs as communicative and activity-centered
rubrics_metrics.description: From the socially-embedded perspective, goals include students engaging in authentic mathematical proving activity as practiced in communities: using proof to justify claims to peers, to explain, to illustrate methods, and to generate and communicate knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional design should situate proof tasks within social activity, encourage peer critique and use of proof to advance collective mathematical work, and study proofs as artifacts that have social meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom norms for presenting and evaluating proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive norms include presenters' responsibilities (explain and defend arguments, respond to questions, highlight high-level ideas, use peer-validated results) and audience responsibilities (read carefully, judge correctness, ask clarifying questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate these norms with students to create learning opportunities; avoid classroom practices where the teacher alone judges correctness and where students are passive consumers of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format should not constrain mathematical reasoning (caution about two-column proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain written formats (e.g., the two-column geometry proof) implicitly constrain teaching and learning by emphasizing premise-to-conclusion testing and discouraging generation of ideas, diagram construction, conjecturing, or choosing premises/conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critical of rigid formats that narrow opportunities for developing generative reasoning; adopt formats and tasks that foster idea generation and exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof's roles in mathematics (explanation, communication, advancing agenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond establishing truth, proofs serve other functions for mathematicians: explanation, pedagogy, illustrating new methods, providing comprehensible accounts, and supplying ideas or techniques for further work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or evaluating proofs, consider these multiple aims; assessment rubrics should include explanatory power, clarity, and potential to advance understanding, not only formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research methodology: allow explanations and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying standards of conviction, participants should be given opportunities to explain and qualify responses so researchers can distinguish absolute conviction from probabilistic belief and detect context-driven answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include follow-up interviews or open explanations in survey/study designs to avoid misinterpreting surface-level responses; this reveals whether problematic responses reflect stable beliefs or contextual artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution: differences between evaluation and construction of arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing arguments and evaluating given arguments are distinct tasks; participants may find it easier to evaluate than to construct, and performance can vary by domain, format (verbal vs symbolic), or exposure to instructional artifacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and assessment should not infer global standards from a single task type; include both construction and evaluation tasks and account for domain/format/context effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learners infer what counts as proof from encountered examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Students generalize classroom norms for proofs from the examples and formats they've repeatedly seen; this shapes their judgments about what constitutes a proof (e.g., rejecting graphical proofs because such proofs weren't modeled in class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To broaden students' conceptions, expose them to varied proof forms and explicitly discuss criteria for acceptability across representations; curriculum should avoid narrow exemplars that limit students' notions of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming uniform mathematician standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians do not unanimously agree on what constitutes acceptable evidence, proof, explanation, simplicity, or clarity; standards of conviction among mathematicians can vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and curricula should recognize heterogeneity in professional practice; do not present a single monolithic standard as the only correct professional norm.
